items.title: Hold work that depends on an unsettled contract
items.description: A frontend-only answer to an open backend question usually gets unpicked later.
items.details: At doctorly, multi-tenancy meant a single practice ID hardcoded across the frontend and a backend design that was still moving. I defined the frontend model first and held the implementation until the contract settled, instead of threading an identifier through every call site and rebuilding it later.

items.title: Stage enforcement instead of waiting for cleanup
items.description: New debt should fail immediately. Old debt should be visible, not hidden.
items.details: Architecture violations had accumulated in shared code. I staged the lint rules from warning to allowlist to error and recorded each existing violation as a file-level exemption, so new violations failed CI from day one and the old ones became a list to work down.

items.title: Fix the cause before adding a layer
items.description: At innn.it the biggest single win was an index.
items.details: Campaign exports that froze dashboards stopped freezing once the indexes matched the read paths. The page-load gain came from server-side rendering, caching, and lighter images. I measure where the time goes before adding a service or a library.

items.title: Say what is delivered and what is not
items.description: A handover is only useful if it states what is still open.
items.details: I handed the Q3 frontend priorities to the next lead in writing: what was settled, what should not be reopened without a concrete reason, and the main risks for Q4. It covered all eight priorities, including the two that had not started.

backgroundHook: I'm **Ansumana Darboe**. Most people call me **Ansu**. I'm a Senior Software Engineer based in **Berlin**. I've built web and mobile software for eight years, and these days my deepest work is frontend architecture on products that are already in production.
The curiosity started with our family computer. I was the kid who took things apart to see what was inside. These days I do the same with large codebases. Fewer missing screws. More late nights.

Before tech, I spent over four years playing professional football and coaching youth teams in **The Gambia**. Our coach had one phrase after any session he considered poor. 'Again tomorrow.' That was it. He picked up his bag and walked off the pitch. I never liked hearing it. I understand it better now.

A knee injury ended the football chapter. I taught in rural classrooms with cracked blackboards and few textbooks. I studied Software Applications at **Gambia Technical Training Institute**, managed networks at **AccounTax Solutions**, and moved to **Berlin** in 2014 without speaking the language or knowing anyone. I believed if I could learn code, I could learn German too.

Since then the work has taken me through very different worlds. I rebuilt the React Native app for real estate teams at **Propstack** and worked on civic platforms at **change.org** and **innn.it**, where a slow page wasn't just an inconvenience. It affected how quickly people could discover, support, and share campaigns. Later I co-founded **ZULA**, a storytelling platform for children who rarely saw themselves reflected in the books they read. I joined **FREY ADV** to work on the frontend rebuild of a practice management system that had run on desktops for over thirty years, and after Frey acquired **doctorly** I moved onto that team. In Q3 2026 I took my turn in the team's frontend lead rotation, setting the quarter's priorities and writing the architecture decisions behind them, before handing over to the next lead in October.

Most days that means **TypeScript** and **React**, with **Node.js** and cloud infrastructure behind them. What I enjoy most is taking a system that already works and making it easier to change without stopping it, and reviewing the code of the engineers doing the same.
Outside of work I still follow football closely. These days my knee prefers that I watch more matches than I play.

growth.title: One real misjudgment, and what changed
growth.description: What it cost the team, and what I changed afterwards.
paragraphs: When I moved onto a new team, I was asked directly whether I knew test-driven development. I said no. They handed me the testing lead for a new module anyway.

I also shipped merge requests that were too large to review properly, and once pushed a change straight to the main branch instead of opening a request for it. Both slowed the team down, including me. Reviewers had to hold a week of changes in their heads at once, and a direct push meant nobody had checked the change before it shipped.

I broke the work into smaller pieces and started taking testing seriously instead of treating it as a step to get through. Within a few months I was writing tests that described what a user does, not just what the code does internally, so they would survive me changing the implementation later.

By the middle of that year I was leading the same kind of testing work I had said no to months earlier, and soon after took my turn in the team's frontend lead rotation. I would rather admit that arc than polish it away.

items.title: doctorly
items.summary: Incremental modernization of doctorly's clinical practice platform after FREY ADV acquired the company. I led the frontend team's priorities during the Q3 2026 rotation and worked directly on state management, observability, and the groundwork for multi-tenancy.
items.description: After FREY ADV acquired doctorly, I moved onto the team building its clinical practice platform. During the Q3 2026 frontend lead rotation I set the quarter's frontend priorities, wrote the architecture decisions behind them, and split ownership across the team. In October I handed the role to the next lead and continued as an engineer on the same codebase.
achievements: Modernized the state-management layer: removed the last Redux usage in favor of React Query and Zustand, and documented the state-ownership rules.
Consolidated seven product areas that each had two frontend implementations, removing roughly 1,100 lines of duplicate code.
Introduced staged architecture dependency rules, enforced in CI.
Implemented and merged production error tracking and Web Vitals monitoring (session-level signals held for Security sign-off) and defined the frontend model for multi-tenancy.
Caught defects in review before merge, such as a validation test that could not fail because it injected its own errors, and a query built in a shape the real endpoint does not accept.
items.problem: doctorly's frontend had accumulated structural debt: leftover Redux alongside newer state patterns, seven product areas with two implementations each, layer boundaries that existed only in documentation, a single practice ID hardcoded throughout, and no frontend error visibility, so production problems reached engineering through support tickets. None of it could be fixed by pausing the product. After the acquisition the team needed a frontend direction: what to fix first, in what order, and how to do it without freezing feature delivery.
solution: Agreed with the team in July to land a few of the quarter's eight frontend priorities properly rather than start all of them. Split ownership three ways: I kept state management, observability, duplicate consolidation, and multi-tenancy; one colleague took architecture and the services migration, another accessibility and CI.

Removed the remaining Redux usage and wrote down who owns which state: server state in React Query, genuinely shared client state in Zustand, everything else local to the component. The guidance went into the repository so reviewers have a written rule to point to.

Consolidated seven product areas that each had two frontend implementations, including Mailbox, LDT, Practice, and Calendar, through six focused merge requests, each leaving a single implementation of its area.

Built on a teammate's entities pilot to turn the documented layer boundaries into ESLint dependency rules, staged from warnings to an allowlist to CI errors. Moved the app-shell layout out of the feature layer, where it had been creating exactly the cross-feature imports the rules exist to prevent.

Wrote the decision record for frontend observability and held implementation until PII handling and the ingestion boundary were agreed with Security and DevOps. Then built error tracking and Web Vitals monitoring as separate merge requests for bootstrap, scrubbing, error capture, and failure behavior, so the privacy work could be reviewed on its own. Documented local setup and troubleshooting so the integration doesn't depend on one person.

Mapped where the frontend assumed a single practice and defined the runtime tenant context, resource ownership, and permission model before writing implementation code. Held implementation until the backend header contract settled; the runtime context API is now merged, and the remaining work depends on platform services the backend is still rolling out.

technicalInsights.title: Fewer Priorities, Finished
technicalInsights.description: We agreed in July to land at least three of the eight priorities properly instead of spreading the team across all of them. Four landed, one had its foundation delivered, one continued under another engineer, and two did not start. The unstarted two were delegated, and I did not have a clear enough signal to tell blocked work from work that had not begun. The cut was deliberate. Losing sight of those two was not.

technicalInsights.title: Enforcing Boundaries Incrementally
technicalInsights.description: By the time enforcement started, 128 violations had accumulated. Fixing them first would have stalled feature work in shared code; excluding whole directories would have hidden them. Instead the rules were staged (warn, then allowlist, then error) and every existing violation became an explicit, file-level exemption. The cost is that the legacy debt stays visible as a list someone has to work down, while new violations fail CI from day one.

technicalInsights.title: Foundation Before Implementation
technicalInsights.description: The frontend hardcoded a single practice ID across 38 call sites while the platform's tenancy design was still changing. Threading a tenant identifier through all of them would have been quick, and probably wrong once the backend settled. Defining the runtime context, ownership, and permission model first meant revising two of those documents as the platform design moved, which is cheaper than revising code. Trade-off: the priority showed no user-visible progress until the backend contract was ready.

technicalInsights.title: Observability Inside Existing Infrastructure
technicalInsights.description: The decision record chose Grafana Faro over Sentry or a hand-built OpenTelemetry setup, so frontend telemetry stays within infrastructure DevOps already runs and already trusts with patient-adjacent data. What we gave up: no packaged issue management or source-map tooling, so release metadata and technical context had to be attached deliberately, and session-level signals stay off until Security signs them off.

outcome.impact: The frontend now has one state-management convention, one implementation per consolidated product area, layer boundaries that CI enforces, and error and performance monitoring built to keep patient data out. Multi-tenancy has a defined model and its first runtime piece merged.
businessResults: Redux fully removed; state-ownership guidance written into the repository.
Seven duplicated product areas consolidated into one implementation each.
Existing architecture violations tracked as explicit exemptions; new dependency violations fail CI.
Production error tracking and Web Vitals monitoring implemented and merged, with session-level signals held for Security sign-off.
Q3 frontend priorities handed to the next lead in writing: what was settled, what was open, and the two main risks for Q4.
Not delivered in Q3: accessibility linting and required CI quality gates (both delegated, neither started), and the services migration, which continues under another owner.

lessonsLearned: Small merge requests keep a change reviewable; they don't make it cheap. Consolidating shared product areas in six focused merge requests still took about four weeks of review, because each one touched code other people were changing.

Delegating a priority is not the same as being able to see it. Two delegated priorities did not move in Q3, and the signals I relied on were not enough to tell blocked work from work that had not started. Next time I would use the existing frontend huddle as an explicit checkpoint for exactly that.

Review load stayed concentrated on me through September, even as the architecture rules matured enough for others to own areas. I made distributing it an explicit action, and by October the incoming lead was reviewing the same merge requests in parallel.
technicalChallengesOvercome: Changed shared foundations while feature delivery continued on top of them: every consolidation and migration step had to be shippable on its own.
Introduced architecture enforcement into a codebase that already broke the rules, without blocking work in flight.
Designed frontend telemetry for a healthcare product, where error context is only useful if patient data stays out of it.
Planned multi-tenancy against a backend and platform design that was still changing during the quarter.

items.problem: A desktop system that had run for more than thirty years carried decades of workflow decisions. solution: Moved the frontend to React and TypeScript domain by domain rather than rewriting it in one step, so improvements could ship incrementally while the legacy services stayed stable.

items.title: ZULA
items.summary: Co-founded a platform for inclusive children's stories. Offline-first for slow networks, 15+ countries, 300+ books distributed.
items.description: Children rarely saw themselves in the stories available to them. As technical co-founder I owned platform architecture, AWS infrastructure, and delivery for a small cross-functional team. We built ZULA mobile-first with React, Node.js, and AWS. Stories had to load on slow networks and survive interrupted connections.
achievements: Led platform architecture as technical co-founder: React, React Native, Node.js, and AWS with offline-first patterns for families on unreliable networks.
Owned AWS infrastructure and CI/CD with Docker and CloudWatch, making deploys routine and reducing AWS costs about 30%.
Mentored a small cross-functional team through delivery and review.
items.problem: Families needed diverse stories on unreliable mobile networks. The constraint: reach children in low-connectivity regions without AWS costs growing faster than the mission.
solution: Chose a modular Node.js + React stack on AWS over a managed BaaS. More setup, but predictable cost and control.
Prioritized offline-first mobile UX: local caching for offline reading and background sync on reconnect, instead of online-only patterns that failed on patchy connections.
Automated Docker deploys early, accepting pipeline complexity during rapid iteration so releases became routine.
Reviewed EC2, S3, and CloudFront usage and cut over-provisioned instances once they showed up in the bill, which brought AWS spend down about 30%.

technicalInsights.title: Cost Control on AWS
technicalInsights.description: EC2, S3, and CloudFront, tuned against the monthly bill. The catch: without cost monitoring from day one, the over-provisioned instances were found late.

technicalInsights.title: Offline-First UX
technicalInsights.description: Local caching for offline reading and background sync on reconnect. Accepted sync conflict handling rather than blocking reads when networks dropped mid-session.

outcome.impact: More children could read stories that reflected their world, even when the connection dropped mid-chapter.
businessResults: AWS costs down about 30% (roughly EUR 300 a month) while CloudWatch reported uptime near 99.9%.

lessonsLearned: What I'd do differently: instrument cost and usage from day one instead of adding monitoring after the first surprising AWS bill. We caught the over-provisioned instances eventually, but an earlier signal would have stretched the runway further.

What I got wrong: the first version of offline sync resolved conflicts by keeping whichever copy synced last, which silently overwrote earlier legitimate edits. I rebuilt it to surface the conflict for a person to resolve, accepting slower syncs for correctness.
technicalChallengesOvercome: Rebuilt offline sync with explicit conflict handling after an early data-loss issue.
Kept content updates working for readers across several countries.

items.question: Who are you and what do you do?
items.answer:
I'm **Ansumana Darboe**, but most people call me **Ansu**. I'm a **Senior Software Engineer** in **Berlin**. My deepest area is **frontend architecture** in React and TypeScript: modernizing established products in healthcare and civic tech while they stay in use.

The most recent work is at **FREY ADV / doctorly**. Before that: civic platforms at **change.org** and **innn.it**, **ZULA**, a startup I co-founded, and a React Native internship at **Propstack**. Details are on [Career](/career) and in the [case studies](/projects).

I've been at **FREY ADV** since **October 2024**, first on the frontend rebuild of **Quincy Mobile**, a practice management system that had run on desktops for more than 30 years. After Frey acquired **doctorly** I moved onto the doctorly team and its clinical practice platform.

The work is frontend foundations: state management, architecture boundaries enforced in CI, production error tracking and Web Vitals monitoring, and the groundwork for multi-tenancy. items.question: How do you approach modernizing a system that is already in production?
items.answer: In steps the product can absorb, never as a rewrite that stops delivery. At doctorly that meant separating server state from UI state instead of extending the old global store, consolidating duplicate implementations one product area at a time, and staging ESLint dependency rules from warning to allowlist to error. Existing violations became a visible list while new ones failed CI immediately. When a change depended on a backend contract that was still moving, I held it rather than build something to throw away. See the [case study](/projects/doctorly).

items.question: How do you handle privacy and security in healthcare software?
items.answer: On the frontend, privacy is mostly about what leaves the browser. For doctorly's production error tracking, keeping patient data out of the telemetry was a design requirement: PII scrubbing is part of how every event is built, telemetry failures cannot break the app, and session-level signals stay off until Security signs them off. In code review I look for places where data crosses a boundary it should not, such as saved filters that were not scoped per user, or a guard that could merge data across patients. Authentication, encryption, and access control sit mostly with the backend and platform teams, and I work against their contracts.

items.title: Performance Optimization: When Your App Starts to Crawl
items.summary: Cutting page load times from eight seconds to under two came down to caching, indexing, and image weight, not clever algorithms. Notes on finding where the time actually goes before optimizing anything.

sections.content: Performance Optimization: When Your App Starts to Crawl

On one project, I worked on cutting page load times from around eight seconds to about a second and a half. The fix was not a clever algorithm. It was server-side rendering, Redis caching for data that did not change between requests, a CDN in front of static assets, and smaller images. Nothing exotic. Each change went through a Lighthouse audit and regression testing, because a speed win that quietly breaks something else is not a win.

That is the pattern I keep running into. Performance problems rarely come from one dramatic bug. They come from doing more work than the situation needs: fetching the same thing twice, re-rendering a tree that has not changed, shipping images nobody has scrolled to yet. Fixing that starts with knowing where the time actually goes, not guessing.
Measure First

You cannot fix what you cannot see, and the slow part is often not where you assumed. Profile before touching code: Chrome DevTools, Lighthouse, or the React Profiler will show you what is actually expensive.

The assumption you walk in with is often wrong. A page that feels slow because of "a heavy component" is just as likely to be waiting on three sequential API calls that could run in parallel. Guessing wastes hours that profiling would have saved in minutes.
The Usual Suspects

Most slowdowns trace back to a short list: too many database round-trips, especially the N+1 kind, rendering more than the screen needs, unoptimized images, algorithms that do more work than the data size justifies, and missing caches. None of these are exotic. They accumulate quietly as a codebase grows, one reasonable-looking change at a time.
Algorithms Matter Less Than You'd Think
Binary search on sorted data is faster than scanning every item, and the difference gets real at scale.

In practice, though, algorithmic complexity matters most when you are processing large in-memory datasets. For most of the web applications I have worked on, the bottleneck has been I/O: the database, the network, the render tree, not the algorithm. Know the tool exists. Do not reach for it before you have measured.
Caching: Don't Do the Same Work Twice

If the same response gets requested repeatedly, store it instead of hitting the database every time. This is where a chunk of that improvement came from: data that did not change between requests moved into Redis, and static assets sat behind a CDN instead of being served fresh on every request.
Cache data that changes infrequently, and be honest with yourself about the TTL. Users notice when a page shows stale data more than they notice a slightly slower load.
Don't Block on I/O

Blocking the main thread on a database call or network request makes the UI feel frozen, even if the actual work only takes a second. async/await keeps things responsive while the request runs in the background.

That example runs the two queries in sequence. If they do not depend on each other, Promise.all runs them in parallel instead, which is often the actual fix behind a slow endpoint once the obvious waste is gone.
Fewer Requests, Lighter Payloads
Combine assets where it makes sense. Defer anything the user has not asked for yet: images below the fold, routes they have not navigated to.
Route-level code splitting keeps the initial bundle small. Nobody downloads the settings page on their way to the homepage.
React-Specific: When Re-renders Are the Problem

React re-renders propagate down the tree by default. React.memo, useMemo, and useCallback skip work when the inputs have not changed, but they carry their own overhead. I reach for them after the profiler shows unnecessary renders, not as a default.
Sprinkling memo across every component adds comparison overhead without fixing anything. Profile first, memoize the component that is actually re-rendering unnecessarily, and leave the rest alone.
For long lists, virtualization matters more than memoization. Rendering a thousand DOM nodes when only twenty are visible is wasted work regardless of how well-memoized each row is.
Database Performance Is Usually the Real Story

Slow queries hurt more than most front-end tweaks combined, and they are often the easiest fix once you find them. On another project, a query against a large collection was taking ten seconds or more, long enough that an export would freeze the dashboard for whoever was running it. Adding an index on the fields the query actually filtered against brought that under a hundred milliseconds. No new caching layer, no rewritten query. Just an index that should have been there.
The other classic shape of this problem is N+1: fetching a list, then fetching related data for each item in a loop instead of one query.

Index the fields you filter and sort on. Avoid N+1 fetches. Use connection pooling so you are not opening a new connection per request. None of this is glamorous, and none of it shows up in a demo, but it is where the time actually goes.
Images Are Usually the Heaviest Thing on the Page
Images dominate page weight more often than anything else. Compress them, serve modern formats like WebP or AVIF where you can, and lazy-load anything below the fold.
A CDN helps once traffic spreads out geographically, but it does not fix an image that is five times larger than it needs to be. Compress first.
Keep Watching After You Ship

Performance degrades quietly as features accumulate. Nobody adds a slow query on purpose; it just happens one reasonable pull request at a time. Track Core Web Vitals, set alerts before users start complaining, and run a Lighthouse audit on a schedule rather than only when something feels off.
What Actually Works

Measure before touching anything. Fix the biggest bottleneck first, which is usually a database query or an unnecessary render, not the thing that looks technically interesting. Cache what does not change often. Compress your images. Add memoization only where the profiler tells you to. Then set up monitoring, because the next slowdown will arrive the same way this one did: quietly, one feature at a time.

items.title: Event-Driven Microservices: When Your App Gets Too Big
items.summary: There was a time deploy took thirty seconds. Then the codebase grew, teams multiplied, and nobody wanted to touch production on a Friday. A walkthrough of splitting a monolith into services that talk through events, with Node.js, Docker, and Kubernetes.

sections.content: Event-Driven Microservices: When Your App Gets Too Big

There was a time deploy took thirty seconds. Then the codebase grew, teams multiplied, and Friday releases became something you avoided. The monolith still worked, mostly. Nobody wanted to be the person who broke it.

Microservices split that pressure into smaller services, each with one job. A user service handles auth. A notification service sends email. When one fails, the others keep running. The tradeoff is more moving parts to watch.

Event-driven architecture is one way to keep those services from tangling. Instead of calling each other directly, they communicate through events. A service announces that something happened. Every other service decides whether that event matters to them.
1. Why Microservices Matter
Fixing a footer typo used to mean deploying the entire application. One database outage could take everything offline. Smaller services limit the blast radius.
Each service does one thing. If payments break, login still works. If email stalls, orders still process. Independence is the point. It is also the cost.
2. How Services Talk to Each Other

When a user signs up, the user service saves the record and publishes UserCreated. Email sends welcome mail. Analytics records the signup. Each listener handles its own failure without blocking the request.
The user service does not need to know who is listening. Publishing an event should feel like dropping a letter into a mailbox. Once it is sent, your work is finished.
Name events after facts, not commands. UserCreated is better than SendWelcomeEmail. Facts age well. Commands get argued about in code review forever.

Events are not a religion. If you need an immediate answer before you can continue, a direct request is fine. A useful rule: if failure in step three should not roll back step one, step three probably should not be inline.
3. From Theory to a Running System

Enough theory. Here is a simple user system: a React frontend, a Node.js backend, Redis Pub/Sub for events, MongoDB for persistence, Docker for local consistency, and Kubernetes for production orchestration.

mkdir event-driven-microservice
cd event-driven-microservice
npm init -y
Project Structure That Makes Sense

Keep the layout simple and domain-focused. Use kebab-case for files, colocate related code, put constants and types in their own files, and keep components thin. Business logic belongs in hooks and utilities, not scattered across JSX.

event-driven-microservice/
├── frontend/
│   ├── src/
│   │   ├── components/
│   │   │   └── create-user-form.tsx
│   │   ├── hooks/
│   │   │   └── use-create-user-form.ts
│   │   ├── helpers/
│   │   │   └── api.ts
│   │   ├── types/
│   │   │   └── user.ts
│   │   └── index.tsx
│   └── package.json
├── backend/
│   ├── src/
│   │   ├── constants/
│   │   │   └── event-channels.ts
│   │   ├── middlewares/
│   │   │   ├── start-app.ts
│   │   │   ├── start-db.ts
│   │   │   └── error-handler.ts
│   │   ├── models/
│   │   │   └── user.ts
│   │   ├── routes/
│   │   │   └── create-user.ts
│   │   ├── events/
│   │   │   └── user-events.ts
│   │   ├── types/
│   │   │   └── user-created-event.ts
│   │   ├── utils/
│   │   │   └── validate-create-user.ts
│   │   └── index.ts
│   └── package.json
├── docker-compose.yml
└── kubernetes/
    ├── frontend-deployment.yaml
    └── backend-deployment.yaml
4. Building the Frontend: Keep It Simple
The frontend collects user data and posts it to the backend. It does not send email, update analytics, or notify a CRM. That belongs elsewhere.

npx create-react-app frontend
cd frontend
npm install axios
Shared Types First
Define request and response shapes once. Avoid any. TypeScript should catch contract drift before runtime does.
API Helper: One Place for HTTP Calls
Centralize HTTP calls in one helper. Read the API URL from the environment so local, Docker, and production stay configurable.
Form Logic in a Hook
Keep the component focused on rendering. Form state, validation, and submit handling live in a custom hook.
The Form Component: Presentation Only
Semantic HTML, labels, and keyboard-friendly controls. The component renders state; it does not own the workflow.
5. Building the Backend: Validate, Persist, Publish
Do not start with routes. Start with responsibilities: validate, persist, publish. Keep route handlers small. Push validation and event wiring into utilities you can test without HTTP.

cd backend
npm init -y
npm install express mongoose redis @godaddy/terminus
npm install -D typescript @types/express @types/node ts-node
Constants and Event Types
Validation Utility
Pure validation functions are easy to test and reuse. Return a message or null instead of throwing inside the validator.
Database Connection: Don't Skip This
Error Handler Middleware
One consistent error response shape beats try/catch copy-pasted in every route.
Server Startup
The Main Server
User Model
This tutorial stores a plain password to stay small. In production, hash with bcrypt or argon2 before save and never return password fields in API responses.
The API Route
Validate. Save. Publish. Return only safe fields. That is the whole handler.
Events: Publishers and Subscribers
Publishers and subscribers stay in one module, but channel names live in constants. Redis Pub/Sub is fine for learning. Kafka or RabbitMQ enter the picture when you need durable replay.
A separate consumer might send welcome email or record analytics. Each can fail independently. Each can be tested with a fake event without booting the whole platform.
6. Docker: Making Deployment Easy
Docker's biggest win is often consistency, not portability alone. "It works on my machine" stops being a category of bug when everyone runs the same containers.

# frontend/Dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]

# backend/Dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3001
CMD ["npm", "start"]
docker-compose: Run Everything Locally

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  frontend:
    build: ./frontend
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      REACT_APP_API_URL: http://localhost:3001/api
    depends_on:
      - backend
  backend:
    build: ./backend
    ports:
      - "3001:3001"
    environment:
      DB_URL: mongodb://mongo:27017/app
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
      PORT: 3001
    depends_on:
      - mongo
      - redis
  mongo:
    image: mongo:7
  redis:
    image: redis:7
docker compose up --build
7. Kubernetes: Managing Your Services at Scale
Running one container is easy. Running many is not. Kubernetes schedules containers, restarts failed pods, and scales replicas. You declare desired state; the cluster enforces it.

# kubernetes/frontend-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: frontend
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: frontend
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: frontend
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: frontend
          image: frontend:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: frontend-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: frontend
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 3000
      targetPort: 3000

# kubernetes/backend-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: backend
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: backend
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: backend
          image: backend:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3001
          env:
            - name: DB_URL
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: app-secrets
                  key: db-url
            - name: REDIS_URL
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: app-secrets
                  key: redis-url
            - name: PORT
              value: "3001"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: backend-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: backend
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 3001
      targetPort: 3001

kubectl apply -f kubernetes/frontend-deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f kubernetes/backend-deployment.yaml
8. What You Should Know Before Going Live
Microservices are not free. They solve some problems and introduce others. Know both sides before you split a monolith.
The Good Stuff

items: Independent deployments: fix one service without breaking others
Team autonomy: different teams can own different services
Fault isolation: one service failure does not kill everything
Scaling flexibility: scale only what needs scaling
Loose coupling through events: add consumers without touching the publisher
Thin components and typed contracts: easier to read, test, and change

sections.content: The Reality Check

items: More complexity: you are managing multiple services instead of one
Network failures: services talking over the network can fail in new ways
Data consistency: keeping state in sync across services is hard
Debugging across boundaries: centralized logs and tracing become essential
Operational overhead: more moving parts means more things to monitor
Events can arrive twice: design consumers to be idempotent
Events can arrive out of order: never assume timing unless you design for it
Security basics matter: hash passwords, hide secrets, validate every input

sections.content: What's Next?
You have a minimal event-driven setup. Extend it with auth, structured logging, monitoring, tests, and a durable broker if replay matters.

items: Hash passwords before persistence if you haven't already
Add authentication and authorization
Implement structured logging and a shared error response format
Set up metrics, traces, and alerting
Write unit tests for validators, publishers, and consumers
Swap Redis for Kafka or RabbitMQ if you need durable replay
Add circuit breakers when calls cross the network

sections.content: A Deep Dive into React
A component that started at fifty lines can grow to five hundred when every feature lands in one file. Understanding React fundamentals helps you split it back apart.
These are the concepts I return to on real projects: components, the virtual DOM, hooks, performance, and state sharing.
1. Components: Your Building Blocks
Components are functions that return UI. Combine a button, a card, and a list into a screen. Data flow and updates happen through props and state.
useState tells React this component remembers a value that can change. Click the button, count updates, only this subtree re-renders.
2. The Virtual DOM: React's Secret Weapon
React does not write to the real DOM on every state change. It diffs a virtual tree and patches the minimum.
Adding one list item updates that row, not the entire list, when keys and structure are correct.
3. Hooks
Hooks brought state and effects to functional components without class lifecycle noise.
useEffect with an empty dependency array runs once on mount. Fetch user data there, store in state, render when ready.
4. Performance: Don't Re-render Everything
Parent re-renders can cascade to children even when their props are identical. memo and useMemo address that when profiling confirms waste.
React.memo prevents re-render when props are shallow-equal.
5. State Management: When Props Aren't Enough
When props drilling gets deep, Context shares data across subtrees. Redux helps when updates are complex and global.
Redux adds structure: actions describe events, reducers compute new state. Reach for Context first; add Redux when complexity demands it.
6. Advanced Patterns: The Pro Moves
Advanced patterns solve specific problems. Adopt them when you hit the problem, not before.
Context suits theme, auth, and locale: data many components read, few components write.
Custom Hooks: Your Secret Weapon
Custom hooks move repeated useEffect and useState logic into one reusable function.
Error Boundaries: Graceful Failure
Error boundaries catch render errors in a subtree and show fallback UI instead of a white screen.
Testing: Don't Skip This
Tests on critical interactions save debugging time later. Start with user-visible behavior, not implementation details.
React Router
React Router maps URLs to components for multi-view single-page apps.
Performance Tips That Actually Matter
Most performance issues are too many renders or too much data at once. Fix those before micro-optimizing.
What You Should Actually Build Next
Build a todo app, a weather fetcher, or a filtered product list. One real project teaches more than reading alone.

A weather app that fetches data from an API and displays it nicely
A small e-commerce product list with filtering and search
A blog with posts, comments, and user authentication
A real-time chat application using WebSockets

sections.content: Final Thoughts
React rewards understanding over memorization. Write working code first, refactor when friction appears.
The community is large. Ask questions when stuck. Every senior engineer started with broken first commits.
Pick one small project and finish it. Completion teaches more than collecting patterns.

items.title: React Hooks: State and Effects Without the Class Boilerplate
items.summary: Before hooks, holding state meant reaching for a class and its lifecycle boilerplate. Notes on useState, useEffect, and knowing when a repeated pattern is actually asking to become a custom hook.

sections.content: React Hooks: State and Effects Without the Class Boilerplate

Before hooks, a functional component could not hold state. If you needed to remember anything between renders, you reached for a class, and the lifecycle methods and boilerplate that came with it piled up fast. Hooks let functions do what only classes used to do: useState remembers a value, useEffect runs code after render, and a custom hook packages logic you would otherwise copy and paste between files.
What a Hook Actually Is

A hook is a function whose name starts with use. That naming convention is not cosmetic. React's linter, and React itself, rely on it to enforce the one real constraint: call hooks at the top level of a component, in the same order, on every render. Break that rule inside a condition or a loop, and React loses track of which piece of state belongs to which useState call.
useState: The One You'll Reach for Most
useState returns a value and a setter. Call the setter, React schedules a re-render, and the component runs again with the new value. That is the whole mechanism. Everything else here builds on it.
useEffect: Work That Happens Outside Rendering

Rendering is supposed to be pure: given the same props and state, it produces the same output, with no side effects. Fetching data, subscribing to an event, or setting a timer are not pure, so they do not belong in the render body. useEffect is where that work goes, and it runs after the browser has painted, not during render.

The cancelled flag matters more than it looks. If userId changes before the first fetch resolves, or the component unmounts mid-request, the effect's cleanup function sets cancelled to true and the stale response gets thrown away instead of overwriting newer state. Skip this and you get a real, hard-to-reproduce bug: a slow response for the old id arrives after a fast response for the new one, and the UI briefly shows the wrong user.
Performance Hooks: useMemo and useCallback

When a render gets expensive, useMemo caches the result of a calculation and useCallback keeps a function reference stable between renders. Both compare their dependency array on every render, so the caching itself is not free. Reach for them once profiling shows the render is actually a problem, not as a default on every function and computed value.
Custom Hooks: Naming the Pattern You Keep Repeating

Look back at the useEffect example above: fetch, track loading, track error, guard against the stale-response case. Needing that same shape in a second component is the signal to extract it, not to retype it.
Same fetch, loading, and error state as before. The difference is it now lives in one place, so a bug fix there fixes every component that uses it, instead of just the one you happened to be editing.
Sharing State Without Prop Drilling: Context

Passing a prop through four layers of components that do not use it, just to reach the fifth one that does, gets old fast. Context lets a provider at the top of a subtree make a value available to anything inside it, no matter how deep.

Context fits values that many components read and few write: theme, the current user, the active locale. It is not a replacement for local state, and reaching for it by default tends to make components harder to test in isolation, not easier.
The Rules, and Why They Exist

Call hooks at the top level, never inside conditions, loops, or nested functions. Only call them from React function components or other hooks. Both rules exist for the same reason: React tracks hook state by call order, not by name. A conditional useState call changes that order between renders, and state silently attaches to the wrong hook.
Where to Start

useState and useEffect cover most of what you need. Add useMemo and useCallback once profiling asks for them, not before. Extract a custom hook the second time you write the same effect, not the fifth. The rules feel like ceremony at first and become invisible once they are habit, the same way you stopped thinking about semicolons.

items.title: React Components, State, and Props: The Building Blocks
items.summary: A React app is small pieces with one job each: a button handles clicks, a card shows a user, a list renders rows. Components, state, and props are how those pieces connect.

sections.content: React Components, State, and Props: The Building Blocks
A React screen is built from small functions that return UI. A button, a card, a list row. You compose them into pages instead of one giant HTML file.
Each component owns one concern. Buttons handle clicks. Cards display records. Lists map data to rows.
1. Components: Your UI Building Blocks
A component is a function that returns markup. Reuse it wherever the same UI appears.
Break the page into focused pieces instead of one file that does everything.
Functional Components: The Modern Way
Functional components are the default. Learn classes only when you maintain older codebases.
Class Components: The Old Way (Don't Worry About These)
Class components still exist in legacy projects. New work should stay in functions with hooks.
2. State: When Your Component Needs to Remember Things
State is what a component remembers. When it changes, React re-renders to reflect the new value.
A counter stores its number in state. Each click updates state and the display follows.
useState: The Hook That Changes Everything
useState returns a value and a setter. Call the setter; React schedules a re-render.
Props: How Components Talk to Each Other
Props pass data from parent to child. The child reads them; the parent owns changes.
3. Props: Passing Data Down
Props are inputs to a component, like function arguments. They flow down, not up.
Simple Props Example
Parent passes message down. Child renders it. One direction keeps data flow traceable.
4. State vs Props: The Key Difference
State is internal and mutable via setters. Props are external inputs the child does not modify.
5. Component Composition: Building Big Things from Small Parts
Combine small components into layouts: header, sidebar, content, footer. Composition scales better than mega-components.
6. Common Patterns You'll Use Every Day
These patterns appear in most apps: fetch on mount, pass results to children, conditional loading states.
7. What You Should Actually Do
Keep components small. Use state for changing data, props for inputs, names that explain intent.

Use functional components with hooks
Use state for data that changes
Use props for data that doesn't change
Give your components and props meaningful names

items.title: The Virtual DOM: React's Secret to Speed
items.summary: Updating the real DOM directly forces the browser to recalculate layout more than you need. React keeps a lightweight copy in memory and only patches what changed.

sections.content: The Virtual DOM: React's Secret to Speed
Touching the real DOM directly triggers layout and paint work across more nodes than you often need. React keeps a lightweight tree in memory and patches only the diff.
1. What the Virtual DOM Actually Is
The virtual tree is a JavaScript representation of UI. React compares the new tree to the previous one and updates the real DOM in minimal steps.
2. Why You Should Care About This
Direct DOM updates rewrite more than necessary. React's diff limits work to changed nodes.
3. How React's Diffing Actually Works
React compares old and new virtual trees, computes a minimal change set, and applies it. That diff step is where much of the performance comes from.
4. The Real Benefits You'll Notice
You describe what the UI should look like. React figures out how to update the DOM. You stop manually tracking every DOM mutation.
5. Keys: The Secret to Efficient Lists
Lists need stable keys so React knows which item moved, changed, or was removed. Without keys, React may re-render more than required.
Use stable unique keys from your data. Avoid array index as key when items reorder or delete.
6. Performance Tips That Actually Matter
React.memo, useMemo, useCallback, and sensible keys reduce unnecessary work. Profile before optimizing.

items: React.memo - prevents components from re-rendering when props haven't changed
useMemo - caches expensive calculations
useCallback - keeps function references stable
Proper keys - helps React track list items efficiently
Avoid creating objects in render - prevents unnecessary re-renders

sections.content: 7. Virtual DOM vs Real DOM: The Real Difference
The virtual tree is plain JavaScript objects. The real DOM triggers layout and paint. React batches updates to reduce thrashing.

items: Virtual DOM is fast because it's just JavaScript objects
Real DOM is slow because it triggers browser reflows and repaints
Virtual DOM lets you think declaratively (what should it look like?)
Real DOM forces you to think imperatively (how do I change it?)
Virtual DOM batches updates for better performance

sections.content: 8. Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
Common mistakes: index keys on dynamic lists, new objects created inside render, over-memoization before measuring.

items: Don't use array indices as keys unless the list never changes
Don't create objects or functions inside render methods
Don't over-optimize - React is already pretty fast
Do use React.memo for components that re-render frequently
Do use useMemo and useCallback when you actually need them

sections.content: 9. Debugging: When Things Go Wrong
React DevTools and the Profiler show which components re-render and how long they take.

items: Install React Developer Tools - it's a major shift
Add console.log to see when components render
Use React Profiler to find performance bottlenecks
Check for missing or duplicate keys in lists
Look for objects being created in render methods

Build a small todo app and watch updates in DevTools. Toggle memo on a hot component and compare render counts.

items: Build a simple todo app and watch how React updates the DOM
Try adding console.log to see when components re-render

Create a list with and without proper keys to see the difference

sections.content: The virtual DOM is engineering, not magic. Understand the diff and keys, and debugging render issues gets straightforward.

items.title: Why I Chose React Over Angular or Vue
items.summary: Angular and Vue are solid choices. React matched how I think about UI: small components, one-way data, and freedom to pick tools as the app grows.

sections.content: Why I Chose React Over Angular or Vue
Angular, Vue, and React all run production software. React matched how I think about UI composition and incremental complexity.
React balanced power and flexibility for the teams I was on. Angular and Vue are solid; this is what fit my workflow.
1. Components as Building Blocks
React components are reusable UI functions. Write a product card once, use it on every listing page.
Angular and Vue have components too. React's function-first model felt natural for the way I split screens.
On an e-commerce site, one ProductCard component replaces copied markup across pages.
2. One-Way Data Flow: No Surprises
React favors one-way data flow: props down, events up. When something breaks, you trace data in one direction.
Two-way binding can be convenient but harder to reason about in large trees. Explicit flow helped me debug faster.
A chat app keeps messages in parent state and passes them to list and input children.
3. Virtual DOM: Smart Updates
React diffs a virtual DOM and patches minimal changes. That matters when lists update frequently.
Vue uses a virtual DOM as well. Angular relies on change detection. I preferred React's predictable update model in the apps I maintained.
A news feed appending posts benefits from targeted updates instead of repainting the whole list.
4. Freedom to Build Your Way
React does not prescribe routing, state, or styling. You add tools as requirements appear.
Angular bundles more opinions upfront, which helps some teams and overwhelms others on day one.
Third-party libraries integrate as components without fighting framework conventions.
5. Great Tools and Community
React DevTools expose component trees, props, and state. That visibility shortened debug sessions.
A large community means most errors have prior art on Stack Overflow or GitHub.
Mix local useState with Redux in the same component when different slices need different scope.
6. Easy to Get Started
You can ship a Hello component on day one and add hooks as features require them.
Angular often expects TypeScript, modules, and DI from the start. React lets you grow into structure.
7. Jobs and Community
React has a large community and strong job market. Meta maintains the core library. When you get stuck, someone has usually hit the same error before.

items: Huge community - someone has solved your problem
Lots of job opportunities
Regular updates from Meta
Tons of tutorials and resources
Great libraries for everything
Active community on Stack Overflow

sections.content: 8. Performance: React Keeps It Fast
React's bundle size and runtime performance are competitive for large apps. React.memo and route-level code splitting keep re-renders and initial load in check.
Memoized list items skip re-render when their props stay the same. That pattern matters on feeds and tables that update often.
Quick Comparison
A quick read on each framework:

items: React: Flexible, great for teams, huge ecosystem, easy to start
Angular: Full-featured, TypeScript-first, lots of built-in stuff, steeper learning curve
Vue: Easy to learn, good for small projects, smaller ecosystem

sections.content: When to Pick Each One
All three are valid choices. Match the framework to team experience, project size, and how much opinionated structure you want upfront.

items: Pick React for: Flexibility, large teams, complex UIs, mobile apps (React Native)
Pick Angular for: Enterprise apps, TypeScript teams, lots of built-in features
Pick Vue for: Small projects, quick prototypes, easy learning curve

sections.content: Final Thoughts
React fit my projects because components stayed small and data flow stayed explicit. If you are still deciding, build the same feature in each framework and notice which one gets out of your way.

entries.title: Who is Ansumana Darboe?
entries.description: Senior Software Engineer in Berlin, deepest in frontend architecture.
entries.response:
Ansumana Darboe (Ansu) is a Senior Software Engineer in Berlin. His deepest area is frontend architecture in React and TypeScript, and most of his work has been on products already in production: healthcare, civic platforms, a startup he co-founded, and a React Native internship.

He currently works at FREY ADV / doctorly on the frontend of a clinical practice platform. In Q3 2026 he took his turn in the team's frontend lead rotation and handed the role to the next lead in October. Before software he played professional football in The Gambia, taught, and worked in IT for a finance office there.

The timeline is on the career page at /career and the case studies are at /projects.

entries.title: What does Ansu do?
entries.description: Modernizing products that are already in use.
entries.response:
He modernizes established products while they keep running. The strongest evidence is the doctorly case study at /projects/doctorly.

His full-stack work covers MongoDB read paths and CI/CD at change.org and innn.it, and the backend and AWS infrastructure at ZULA.

entries.title: How does Ansu run projects?
entries.description: Watch first, ship in small steps, say early when something slips.
entries.response:
Before changing a workflow, he watches someone use it. At FREY ADV that was forty minutes with a doctor, and it shaped the first weeks of work.

He ships in steps that can roll back on their own, records decisions that affect how others work in the pull request, and holds work that depends on an unsettled backend contract instead of building a stopgap. He also names his own early mistakes: merge requests too large to review, and one change pushed straight to the main branch. The full account is on the About page.

entries.title: Where did Ansu grow up?
entries.description: From The Gambia to Berlin in 2014.
entries.response: Ansu is from The Gambia and grew up in a village there. He moved to Berlin in 2014 without speaking German or knowing anyone.

entries.title: What is Ansu's journey?
entries.description: Timeline from GTTI to doctorly.
entries.response:
2008: starts studying Software Applications at GTTI in The Gambia. 2011 to 2013: IT for a finance team at AccounTax Solutions. 2014: moves to Berlin. 2018 to 2019: full-stack program at the Digital Career Institute, where he ships the Buildy app. 2019: three-month React Native internship at Propstack. 2020 to 2023: full-stack developer at change.org e.V. and then innn.it. 2023 to 2024: technical co-founder of ZULA. 2024 to now: FREY ADV, first on Quincy Mobile and then on doctorly's clinical practice platform.

The full timeline with case study links is on the career page at /career.

entries.title: How did Ansu get into software?
entries.description: From teaching and IT support to a full-stack career.
entries.response: He taught in rural classrooms in The Gambia and studied Software Applications at GTTI from 2008, then worked in IT at AccounTax Solutions. In Berlin he took a full-stack program at the Digital Career Institute from 2018 to 2019 and shipped the Buildy app during it. The timeline is on /career.

entries.title: How did football shape Ansu's approach to teamwork?
entries.description: Four years as a professional, then youth coaching.
entries.response: He played professionally in The Gambia for more than four years, won two domestic trophies, and coached youth teams. A knee injury ended his playing career. He still follows the game closely.

entries.title: What did Ansu learn from teaching?
entries.description: A nursery school and rural classrooms before IT.
entries.response: Before IT he ran Neil Williams Nursery School in The Gambia (September 2005 to May 2008) and taught in rural classrooms with very few materials.

entries.title: How did Ansu start his tech career in The Gambia?
entries.description: IT for a 50-person finance team in The Gambia.
entries.response: At AccounTax Solutions LLC (July 2011 to April 2013) he ran IT for a 50-person finance team: networks, file servers, workstations, and internet access for 100+ internal and external stakeholders. He trained colleagues on software and workflows and set up security policies and monitoring for sensitive finance data.

entries.title: What was it like moving to Berlin?
entries.description: Berlin in 2014 without German.
entries.response: He moved to Berlin in 2014 without speaking German. He studied German at BSI Berlin from 2016 to 2018 and reached C1, then trained as a full-stack developer at the Digital Career Institute.

entries.title: What are Ansu's recent projects?
entries.description: Five case studies, starting with doctorly.
entries.response: The case studies, in the order he would point to them: doctorly (frontend modernization of a clinical practice platform), Quincy Mobile (the frontend rebuild of a 30-year-old desktop practice system), ZULA (an offline-first children's reading platform he co-founded), change.org / innn.it (civic petition platforms under campaign traffic), and Propstack (a three-month React Native internship). All five are at /projects.

entries.title: What is the Quincy Mobile project?
entries.description: A 30-year-old desktop practice system, rebuilt as a web application.
entries.response:
At FREY ADV he joined to work on the frontend rebuild of Quincy Mobile, a practice management system that had run on desktops for more than 30 years, built in React and TypeScript and migrated domain by domain so practices kept working. He started with forty minutes next to a doctor.

After Frey acquired doctorly he moved onto doctorly's clinical practice platform. See /projects/quincy and /projects/doctorly.

entries.title: What did Ansu do at change.org and innn.it?
entries.description: Full-stack work on petition platforms under campaign traffic.
entries.response: At change.org e.V. (2020 to 2022) and innn.it (2022 to 2023) he worked full-stack on petition and campaign flows. At change.org, API and MongoDB tuning cut response times on core flows by about 40%. At innn.it, petition pages went from about 8 seconds to about 1.5 with server-side rendering, Redis and CDN caching, and lighter images, and reworked indexes took some queries from over 10 seconds to under 100 ms. Organic traffic grew from about 50,000 to 100,000+ monthly visitors, a team result he contributed to. See /projects/innnit.

entries.title: What is ZULA?
entries.description: An offline-first reading platform he co-founded.
entries.response:
ZULA (July 2023 to September 2024) was an offline-first reading platform for children who rarely saw themselves in the books available to them. He was technical co-founder and built it with React, React Native, Node.js, MongoDB, and AWS. It reached families in 15+ countries, raised EUR 20,000, partnered with Audible, distributed 300+ books, and placed third of 100+ entrants at the Afro German Startup Pitch 2024.

The first version of offline sync kept whichever copy synced last, which overwrote earlier edits. He rebuilt it to surface the conflict for a person to resolve. See /projects/zula.

entries.title: What did Ansu do at Propstack?
entries.description: A three-month React Native internship.
entries.response: In a three-month internship (April to June 2019) he worked on the React Native app for real estate field teams: prefetching and skeleton loaders instead of blank screens on the listing screens, offline support so agents did not lose changes on patchy signal, the iOS and Android defects behind the most support tickets, and the documentation the codebase was missing. See /projects/propstack.

entries.title: What is the Buildy mobile app?
entries.description: A mobile app shipped during the Digital Career Institute program.
entries.response: Buildy is a construction workflow app he shipped during the Digital Career Institute program. It reached more than 1,000 downloads and a 4.2-star rating.

entries.title: What are Ansu's technical skills?
entries.description: Frontend first, then the backend and infrastructure around it.
entries.response: Frontend is where he goes deepest: TypeScript, React, Next.js, React Native, Tailwind CSS, with React Query and Zustand for state. The backend side is Node.js, Express, MongoDB, and Redis, mostly from change.org, innn.it, and ZULA. Infrastructure is AWS, Docker, Kubernetes, and CI/CD. He would not present himself as a backend specialist.

entries.title: What has Ansu led?

entries.response: In Q3 2026 he took his turn in the frontend lead rotation at doctorly and handed over to the next lead in writing; /projects/doctorly has the detail. At ZULA he was technical co-founder. Day to day he reviews the team's merge requests and pairs on architecture work. His title is Senior Software Engineer.

entries.title: How does Ansu handle cloud and DevOps?
entries.description: Infrastructure he has owned: ZULA on AWS.
entries.response: At ZULA he owned the infrastructure: Docker and CloudWatch made deploys routine, and AWS spend came down about 30% (roughly EUR 300 a month). At innn.it, Docker and Kubernetes pipelines cut deploy time by about 55%. His first job was IT administration for a finance team, which is where he learned what an outage costs the people waiting on it.

entries.title: What does Ansu work on in healthcare software?
entries.description: Frontend foundations for a clinical practice platform.
entries.response: At doctorly he works on frontend foundations: state management, architecture boundaries enforced in CI, production error monitoring, and the frontend model for multi-tenancy. See /projects/doctorly.

entries.title: How does Ansu approach performance?
entries.description: Measure where the time goes, then fix the cause.
entries.response: He measures where the time goes before changing anything. At innn.it the biggest single win was an index: some queries on the largest MongoDB collections went from over 10 seconds to under 100 ms. Petition pages there went from about 8 seconds to about 1.5 with server-side rendering, caching, and lighter images. At Propstack, prefetching and skeleton loaders replaced blank screens.

entries.title: How does Ansu report impact?

entries.response: He prefers numbers he can explain: baseline, method, timeframe, and whose work it was. The innn.it query work was his own change. The innn.it organic traffic growth was a team result he contributed to, and the case study says so. See /projects/innnit.

entries.response: He studied Software Applications at the Gambia Technical Training Institute from 2008 to 2010: C, C++, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and databases. It was his first formal exposure to programming.

entries.response: He studied German at BSI Berlin from 2016 to 2018 and reached C1. He passed the Leben in Deutschland test with 33 out of 33 and uses German in Berlin every day.

At the end of his Q3 2026 frontend lead rotation he handed over in writing, including what should not be reopened without a concrete reason and the main risks for Q4.

stateBoundary.title: How screen state splits
stateBoundary.intro: The clinical screen reads from two separate stores instead of one shared state tree.

serverState.label: Server state · React Query
serverState.body: Patient records, appointments, documents. Fetched from the network, cached, and retried automatically when the connection drops.

uiState.label: UI state · Zustand
uiState.body: Form drafts, selected tabs, open filters. Lives in the browser and keeps working even when the network doesn't.

stateBoundary.closing: Only the server-state half waits on the network. A slow connection blocks data, not the screen.
